Top News
 
 
 
 Moment of reckoning 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 There's financial trouble brewing in Europe again, but a new decade is bringing a fresh group of casualties. In the 2010s, the crowd who landed in hot water was known as the PIIGS, which stood for Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain. This time around, it's moving north, impacting countries like France, Germany, and the United Kingdom.  Euro drops to 17-month low  

 What happened? Take a look at the growth rates. Spain's economy grew at a solid 2.8% in 2025, and Greece grew at 2.1%—double or even triple the rate of the U.K. and France. In fact, Southern Europe is emerging as the continent's economic bright spot, while Europe's "Big Three" northern economies are bogged down by serious problems. Germany's industrial pillar has been compromised by the lack of cheap Russian gas and flatlining exports to China; political volatility and persistent inflation continue to plague the U.K., while rising rates and fiscal deadlock are hounding France, where massive deficits and total public debt near 120% of GDP.

"If we don't act, there is indeed a risk of being gradually strangled by rising interest rates," declared Emmanuel Moulin, governor of the Banque de France. "We have to remain masters of our own destiny." Borrowing premiums have gotten out of hand in France, with yields jumping higher than any other G7 country since the Iran war began, forcing Paris to pay even more than comparable debt from Rome or Athens. 

Things aren't better in London. "The truth is [Britain's] skating on pretty thin ice in fiscal terms, and nothing would be worse both economically and politically than if the ice were to crack beneath our feet," added Andy Haldane, former chief economist of the Bank of England. "That is the Achilles' heel of this government. Unless and until action is taken on that, [Prime Minister Andy Burnham] will remain, alas, in hock to the bond market." 

 Thought bubble: The situation is not only impacting fixed-income traders and sentiment, but changing the political landscape. Given public finance instability and other crises, like immigration and the cost of living, there has been a shift toward parties like Reform UK, National Rally (RN), and the Alternative for Germany (AfD). The outlook can become even more emboldened when unbridled pluralism is preached over a proud national identity, or in response to entities that refer to these feelings as fringe stances and populist anger. ( 4 comments )
